prompt: Graph fundamentals — which two statements are correct?
options: A finite graph consists of a finite number of nodes and a finite number of edges.
A finite graph consists of a finite number of nodes but may have infinitely many edges.
The edge set of a *directed* graph is defined as E := V×V such that (u,v) ∈ E ⇔ (v,u) ∈ E.
The edge set of an *undirected* graph is defined as E := V×V such that (u,v) ∈ E ⇔ (v,u) ∈ E.
explanation: Finitely many nodes bound the number of possible edges by |V|² ✓✗. Symmetry is exactly the defining property of undirected edges ✓, whereas a directed graph explicitly permits (u,v) ∈ E without (v,u) ∈ E ✗.

prompt: Graph algorithms (BFS/DFS) — which two statements are correct?
options: Breadth-first search can be used to determine shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Depth-first search must use a queue to manage the open nodes.
In an undirected graph G, DFS produces only tree edges and back edges.
BFS always traverses fewer nodes than DFS, for every input.
explanation: BFS explores in layers, so its tree distances are exactly the unweighted shortest-path distances ✓. In an undirected graph every edge is seen from both endpoints, which excludes forward and cross edges ✓. DFS uses a *stack* (explicit or the call stack) ✗, and a full traversal visits every reachable node either way ✗.

prompt: Graph algorithms (trees, topological sort, DFS on a DAG) — which two statements are correct?
options: If a connected undirected graph with n nodes has n−1 edges, it must be a tree.
On a fully connected directed graph, topological sort does not terminate.
A preorder traversal of a min-heap outputs the elements in sorted order.
During a depth-first search of a directed acyclic graph, cross edges can occur.
explanation: Connected ∧ exactly n−1 edges ⇔ acyclic ⇔ tree — a classic equivalence ✓. A DAG has no back edges but may certainly have forward *and* cross edges ✓. Topological sort on a cyclic graph still terminates; it merely reports failure ✗, and a heap has no left/right ordering, so preorder is not sorted ✗.

prompt: Graph representations — which two statements are correct?
options: An adjacency list needs Θ(V+E) space; an adjacency matrix needs Θ(V²).
The adjacency matrix answers "is (u,v) an edge?" in O(1), the adjacency list in O(deg(u)).
The adjacency list is preferable for dense graphs, the matrix for sparse ones.
Converting between the two representations costs Θ(V + E).
explanation: The space bounds ✓ and lookup costs ✓ are the defining trade-off. The recommendation is inverted — lists suit *sparse* graphs, matrices *dense* ones ✗ — and the conversion has to touch all V² matrix cells, so it is Θ(V²) ✗.

prompt: You need the shortest path by number of edges between two nodes of an unweighted graph. Which statement is correct?
options: BFS solves this in Θ(V+E), since it explores the graph in layers outward from the source.
DFS solves this in Θ(V+E), since it explores every path to its end.
Only Dijkstra solves this, because shortest paths always require a priority queue.
This requires Bellman-Ford, since the edge count can be negative.
explanation: BFS's layer-by-layer expansion means a node is discovered exactly when the fewest possible edges have been used, so dist[] holds unweighted shortest distances. DFS may reach a node via a long detour first. Dijkstra would work but is unnecessary overhead, and edge counts are never negative.

prompt: BFS and DFS compared — which two statements are correct?
options: Both run in Θ(V+E); they differ in exploration order, not in asymptotic cost.
BFS uses a queue (FIFO), DFS a stack (LIFO) — explicitly or via recursion.
DFS is asymptotically faster than BFS on sparse graphs.
BFS computes finishing times, which are the basis for topological sort and SCCs.
explanation: Identical asymptotics ✓ and the FIFO/LIFO contrast ✓ are the essentials. Neither is asymptotically faster ✗, and it is *DFS* whose finishing times drive topological sort and the SCC algorithm ✗.

prompt: DFS edge classification — which two statements are correct?
options: An edge (u,v) with v coloured GRAY is a back edge and closes a cycle.
For v BLACK, u.disc < v.disc gives a forward edge and u.disc > v.disc a cross edge.
An edge (u,v) with v coloured WHITE is a cross edge.
Back edges can occur in a DAG.
explanation: GRAY = an ancestor still on the recursion stack ⟹ back edge ⟹ cycle ✓, and the disc-time comparison separates forward from cross edges ✓. WHITE means first discovery, i.e. a *tree* edge ✗, and a back edge would prove a cycle, which a DAG has none of ✗.

prompt: Topological sort via DFS — where is each finished vertex placed in the output list?
options: At the front of the list, so the whole sort costs Θ(V+E).
At the end of the list, so the result must be reversed afterwards.
At the position given by its discovery time.
Sorted by vertex label, after the DFS completes.
explanation: A vertex finishes only after all its descendants have finished, so prepending each finished vertex places it before everything reachable from it. Front-insertion into a linked list is Θ(1), leaving the total at Θ(V+E).

prompt: Topological sort — which two statements are correct?
options: It is only defined for directed acyclic graphs.
It orders the vertices so that u precedes v for every edge (u,v).
The topological order of a DAG is always unique.
It is computed with BFS, using the finishing times of the queue.
explanation: A cycle makes a consistent linear order impossible, so DAG-only ✓, and the ordering condition ✓ is the definition. Several valid orders usually exist (any two incomparable vertices may swap) ✗, and the algorithm is built on DFS finishing times ✗.

prompt: The SCC algorithm — which two statements are correct?
options: It runs DFS, computes the transpose Gᵀ, then runs DFS on Gᵀ visiting vertices by descending finishing time from the first pass.
Its total cost is Θ(V+E), since it is two DFS passes plus building the transpose.
Two different strongly connected components may share a vertex.
The second DFS pass visits the vertices in ascending finishing time.
explanation: The two-pass scheme with the transpose ✓ costs Θ(V+E) ✓. SCCs are maximal and therefore always disjoint ✗, and the order in the second pass is *descending* finishing time — ascending would not produce the components ✗.

prompt: Effect of adding or removing a single edge on the number of SCCs — which two statements are correct?
options: Adding an edge can only decrease or maintain the number of SCCs, never increase it.
Removing an edge can only increase or maintain the number of SCCs, never decrease it.
Adding a single edge can merge at most two SCCs into one.
Removing an edge can split an SCC into at most two components.
explanation: A new edge can only create new mutual reachability ⟹ merges only ✓; deleting one can only destroy it ⟹ splits only ✓. Both "at most two" claims are false ✗✗: in the lecture's 10-node example one added edge threads a cycle through four components at once, and removing 8→5 splits {5,8,9} into three singletons.

prompt: Eulerian circuits in a strongly connected directed graph — which two statements are correct?
options: A necessary condition is that in-degree equals out-degree at every vertex.
A greedy walk from an arbitrary start always closes back at the start, but need not cover all edges.
An Eulerian circuit visits every *vertex* exactly once.
A single greedy walk always yields a complete Eulerian circuit.
explanation: Each visit consumes one incoming and one outgoing edge ⟹ the degree condition ✓, and the same argument shows the walk can only get stuck at the start ✓ — though edges elsewhere may remain, which is why cycles have to be spliced together ✗. Visiting every *vertex* once is a Hamiltonian circuit; Eulerian is about *edges* ✗.
